rationale: Design-based critical machine learning program for children aged 9-13, who built ML robots for social good and were assessed with pre/post drawings and responses.
Interviews with Korean leading AIED teachers on curriculum and learning design for student-AI collaboration, including teaching AI principles and ethics, in K-12 schools.
PD program giving K-12 science teachers explanations of how AI makes decisions to improve trust in AI-EdTech; experiments plus discourse analysis.

On-the-job teacher training (mostly student teachers) on a STEAM pedagogical concept that links robotics, coding and AI to the SDGs, delivered in 7th grade classrooms. AI teacher training makes it A. No pre/post or comparison is described.
Examines AI curricula for kindergarten children (aims, content, methods, evaluation) drawing on previous studies; AI literacy of young children is A; reads as a synthesis of prior work.
Conceptual argument for children aged 7-11 to become aware of AI bias and values in co-creational spaces.
Youth produce media about AI in an ethics-centered pedagogy; examines their understanding of AI and design features of the pedagogy; only youth named so secondary_unspecified; no pre/post.
Survey of university students on how well they learn with AI technology applications, and which factors predict it. This is use of AI, not AI literacy.
Text and opinion systematic review on including AI in radiology curricula for health-science students; covers both teaching AI and AI tool use, A taken.
Medical students used the BioWorld ITS, and their think-aloud data were collected and analysed for cognitive load during SRL.
Scoping review of AI literacy research in higher and adult education.
High school students take an introductory AI course that teaches AI topics, and the study compares two group sizes. Learning about AI makes it A.

Two-year AI curriculum for high school students built and iteratively tested with student feedback over three years; students program embedded AI on smartphones (project work, no design process stated).
Children at a museum used an AI-based interactive guidance exhibit; learning compared against a matched conventional exhibit.

Ninth graders aged 13 to 14 discuss in groups with a conversational agent (an expert or peer role) or with no agent. The study looks at the effect on discussion and systems thinking, so it is B. I took the stage from the ages.
Fifth and sixth graders used the HINTS ITS in flexibility training; pre/post problem-solving tests in a quasi-experiment.
Review of AI and learning analytics in teacher education, including teachers' perceptions and digital competence regarding AI. With A and B content together, the record is coded A.
Position paper defining the metaverse and AI's role in metaverse education; no learners, no AI literacy, no tool-use study.
Systematic review of AI-supported teaching and learning in early childhood, including ethical implications.

Pre-service teachers learn in their own university course with an AI chatbot that gives feedback. The study measures the effect on performance and motivation, not AI literacy, so it is B. The chatbot type is not stated, so the subtype is other. The level they will teach is not stated.

Learners used gamified tutoring environments in a factorial experiment with a control environment, measuring stereotype-threat effects. Participants were a mix of high-school and undergraduate students.
Pre-service teachers' perceptions and intentions to use chatbots for learning during training; acceptance-type study with questionnaires, interviews and behaviour analysis.

Systematic review of studies that use AI robots for instruction, focused on learning performance. Participants range from school to professional and higher-education settings, so the audience is unclear.
The AI is a back-end risk-detection system that triggers nudges for online university learners. Learners never deal with the AI directly, so the record is C.
Undergraduates use a fuzzy-based ITS that teaches programming, and their data were collected here, so it is B with the its_adaptive subtype. The evaluation uses experiments and t-tests.
High school groups interacted with two chatbot agent designs in a biology lesson, and their discussion patterns were compared.
Customer service chatbot anthropomorphism experiments; outside education.
Human-AI relationship model with social chatbot Replika among general populations; no learning context, so C outside education.
Develops an analytic rubric for ML-based scoring of high school physical science responses; AI is a back-end scoring method, so C.
Design and development of a mobile moral education game for primary schools; AI algorithms are only a back-end component.
ML course for low-SES middle and high school students who understood ML and built an image classification model via a human-centered process.

Studies how Swedish K-12 teachers understand AI and what misconceptions they hold, using the Intelligent TPACK framework, so it is A. A questionnaire and focus groups were analysed by qualitative content analysis.
An ML learning intervention for middle school students in Nigeria. It tracks how their understanding of ML, ethical awareness and view of societal impact change, using pre-post open-ended surveys.

An ethnography of preschool children's play with a robot, with interviews on how they understand and imagine AI and robots, including critical boundaries. This is the children's AI understanding, so it is A.
Conceptualizes and measures primary teachers' AI readiness (cognition, ability, vision, ethics); teachers' understanding of AI is A; large-sample PLS-SEM survey.

In teen workshops, participants tinker with makeup to fool facial recognition. The study analyses how they make sense of the technical and political sides of AI, which is critical, justice-centred AI literacy, so it is A.
Interviews with in-service language teachers about their attitudes and concerns on AI-assisted language learning, including ethics. The level they teach is not stated.
Two-year pilot developing and evaluating an experiential AI-readiness curriculum for student-teachers covering AI misbehaviour and bias; teacher AI training is A; no pre/post or comparison reported.
Argument essay on teaching students to question and critique GenAI as a learning tool, across levels from primary to tertiary.
Workshops and survey on students', teachers' and institutions' concerns about AI ethics in distance higher education.
Systematic review of the ethics of AI in education, covering guidelines, capacity building and teacher training for ethical use. No specific K-12 audience is stated.
Conceptual pedagogy for university learners to understand AI as a black box, including its social and ethical boundaries.
Document analysis of ChatGPT in schoolteacher education for lesson planning, with critical evaluation of limitations. Counted as GenAI teacher training, so A.

Technology probe of AI-supported classroom orchestration (pairing policies) in a middle school; students and teachers used it and gave feedback; design exploration with reactions only, no outcome test.
TAM-based acceptance study of a scripted AI robot teacher among elementary pupils; acceptance studies are B; robot so robot_agent; questionnaire plus SEM is a survey.
Framework paper on AI as a back-end for learnersourcing systems. No learner use is studied and there is no K-12 signal.
Learners worked together with a pedagogical conversational agent, and their behaviour was recorded and related to performance. The abstract gives no K-12 signal and no pre/post or comparison group.
Position paper on conversational agents administering assessments to boost test-taking effort; agent type unstated.
Conceptual framework for NLP as the back-end of peer-feedback support in higher education. No learners used it in this study.
A UTAUT2 acceptance study of ChatGPT use among higher-education students, so it is B with the genai subtype.
Pilot evaluation of ChatGPT's impact on L2 writing learners; framed as tool effect so B genai; no K-12 signal; qualitative approach.
Doctoral students' views on how ChatGPT affects their L2 writing, gathered qualitatively.
A conceptual discussion, built on existing literature, of the potential and problems of ChatGPT in education. It does not name an audience.
Medical students actually used the BioWorld ITS with logs collected; the focus is their self-regulated learning behaviours while using it, which v2 codes A; process mining fits no listed method.
Undergraduates use an argumentative chatbot in class debates. The study measures the effect on argumentation skills and motivation, so it is B. The chatbot type is not stated.
Language teachers used ChatGPT for instruction; study examines their pedagogical judgement, roles and raising AI ethical awareness; teaching level not stated.
Experiment on social robot anthropomorphism and empathy in general participants; not education.
A systematic review of digital game-based English learning in preschool and primary school. AI appears only as a recommended future technology, so it is C. The review covers several levels.
Survey of non-western AI ethics guidelines and intercultural ethics argument; society-level, not education, so C.
An editorial for a special issue that summarises 11 papers on AI in education across mixed themes. The audience is not stated, and it is unclear whether it is A or B.
Meta-analysis pooling Korean studies on how well school AI education works; learning about AI, so A.
Delphi-based development and CFA validation of a K-12 teacher AI competence self-efficacy scale covering knowledge, pedagogy and ethics.
Develops and validates a scale of teachers' readiness for AI applications, including self-efficacy and ethical awareness; teaching level not stated.
Grade 9 students' perceptions of an AI teammate (trust in and capability of AI) during problem solving. This is how students understand and work with AI, not the tool's effect.
Review of AI in primary education that covers both learning AI/ML concepts and using AI tools. With A and B content together, the record is coded A.
Quasi-experiment with sixth graders on conceptual change about AI using a two-tier test approach, experimental vs control group.
Hands-on ML activities for secondary school students analysed via interviews and screen recordings for CT development.

Analyses university students' interaction patterns with a chatbot tutor in relation to self-regulated learning phases; how students use AI (self-regulation while using) is A under v2; log/pathway analysis fits no listed method.
Short conceptual article on the ethics and governance of generative chatbots in higher education (privacy, bias, plagiarism, policy).
An AIoT platform used to teach AI concepts to first-year university students. One-group pre/post test of AI understanding.
Conceptual framework for AI literacy assessment with generic, domain-specific and ethics parts; it names professional domains but no school students or teachers, so class and audience are unknown.
EFL teachers design chatbot-integrated lesson plans analysed through TPACK, including judging the chatbot's limitations; AI-TPACK and teachers' judgement of AI is A; teaching level not stated.
Young learners create AI-based robots with an ICAP strategy; quasi-experiment with control group on CT, motivation and gender.
Questionnaire on university art teachers' attitudes and self-efficacy toward AI; AI-literacy-type content but higher-education audience.
Quantitative survey with SEM of the AI literacy dimensions (knowledge, ethics and others) of pre-service teachers.
A critical framework for questioning LLMs, aimed at the general public's literacy rather than at a school or education setting. It is conceptual.
How higher-education students with disabilities use and perceive ChatGPT; how-students-use is A under v2; interviews.
Higher-education students' (vs public) perceptions of risks and damages of AI academic performance prediction; learners' understanding of AI risk is A; online survey.
Studies how chemistry and sports students query ChatGPT during decision-making, which is how students use AI. Nothing signals K-12, so the audience is unknown.
Develops a scale for university students' fear of being without AI. This concerns reliance on AI, so A.

GenAI workshops and courses for university professors (GenAI teacher training is A); method order puts review first since a literature review is part of the methodology, though workshops with surveys and observations follow.

A project-based AI literacy course for senior secondary students, evaluated with mixed methods. The post-course test, self-surveys and focus groups cover applying AI concepts and AI ethics. Only a post-course test is described.
Middle and high school students learned math with a scaffolding chatbot vs traditional hints in ASSISTments; chatbot type unstated.
Focus groups with K-12 teachers on how they would collaborate with AI in instruction, and on barriers. This is teachers' understanding of AI.
UTAUT2 acceptance study of chatbots among K-12 teachers. Acceptance studies are B, and the chatbot type is not stated.

Middle school students in China receive immediate AI-generated feedback from automated scoring of scene descriptions and revise their work. The study measures the effect on quality, so it is B. Scores were compared before and after revision.
Six-year-olds in a primary school use an AI object-recognition app with Cuisenaire rods to learn mathematics. Video interaction analysis looks at their learning with the tool, so it is B.
Secondary mathematics teachers' awareness and perceptions of ChatGPT and of integrating it into teaching. This is their understanding and judgement of AI rather than acceptance modelling.
Within-subjects experiment on how ChatGPT-simplified texts affect university EFL students' reading comprehension.
A UTAUT2 acceptance survey of ChatGPT among higher-education students, so it is B with the genai subtype.
Acceptance study (perceived ease of use, usefulness, intention to use) of AI educational applications among pre-service teachers; acceptance studies are B.
Conceptual classification of GenAI tools to help educators design inquiry-based lesson plans; focus on tool utility, no participants.
Perception and motivation survey of university design students about ChatGPT. It is acceptance-like, so B.
English teachers' perceptions of ChatGPT's benefits and concerns, which is their understanding of AI. The teaching level is not stated, and 'academic ranks' hints at higher education.
A systematic review of how ChatGPT is applied in academic settings, which are mostly higher education. It covers the use of the tool, so it is B with the genai subtype.
In-service EFL teachers learned over a semester to integrate ChatGPT into lesson planning and microteaching, which counts as GenAI teacher training. The level they teach is not stated.
Conjoint survey experiment on which AI tool features university students prefer; a preference/acceptance-type study.
2x2 experiment in higher education on how students perceive LLM versus educator feedback. Only perceptions were measured, with no learning outcome.
Sixth graders learned science in AR with GenAI pedagogical agents, compared against a control group, measuring achievement and cognitive load.
Fifth graders taught a teachable Q&A agent in a reading program. The study measures the effect on reading interest and engagement.
Effect of ITS use on programming performance of students; no K-12 signal so audience unknown; mixed methods with no pre/post or control group stated.
Systematic SWOT review of using ChatGPT in teaching and learning and its effect on outcomes. No audience level is stated.

A longitudinal survey of how often undergraduates interact with generative AI chatbots and the effect on their learning autonomy. It looks at the effect of the tool, so it is B with the genai subtype.
A case study of teachers using ChatGPT to write scenarios for scenario-based learning, with a focus on the quality of the generated product, so it is B. Nothing signals K-12.
Online experiment comparing learning from AI-generated versus human-made videos for a management course; learners not identified as K-12.
Phenomenological study of how ChatGPT use supported university EFL students' L2 development.
Interviews on EFL teachers' emotions in GenAI-based classes, framed by TAM; reaction to tool use, teaching level not stated.
Meta-analysis of the effect of chatbot use on language learning; tool effect is B; ChatGPT named so genai taken first; no K-12 signal.

Students in a Java programming course receive LLM-generated or instructor feedback, assigned at random, and the study compares perceptions and score gains. Nothing signals K-12, so the audience is unknown.
Instructors used ChatGPT to build a Master's-level course; focus on the product and efficiency of course design.
How university students choose between ChatGPT and Google when seeking academic help. This is how students use AI, so A under v2.
Interviews with postgraduate EAP students on how ChatGPT affected their language-learning needs.
Undergraduate students' perceptions of a chatbot-based learning environment in a course, using mixed data. Only perceptions and acceptability were measured; the chatbot type is not stated.
UTAUT-style survey of preservice teachers' intention to use AI in lesson planning. Acceptance studies count as B.
A GPT-4 chatbot was developed to support doctoral students' synopsis writing, as an exploratory case. No pre/post or comparison group.
Quasi-experiment comparing writing feedback from AI (Poe) with teacher feedback, among undergraduates. It measures the tool's effect.
University EFL students used ChatGPT-supported argumentation compared with a conventional group; the study looks at the tool's effect on argumentation.
A university student's argumentation with ChatGPT on calculus concepts was analysed for how well ChatGPT supports learning. The focus is the tool's support, not AI literacy.
An AI-based career education program was delivered to high-school students with intellectual disabilities, with effects measured by a single-group pre/post design.
A systematic review of educational research that uses XAI methods such as SHAP and LIME to explain models. The AI is a research or back-end method.
Researchers prompt ChatGPT to score writing with varied demographic descriptors to test bias; LLM output judged by researchers only, nobody learning, so C.
A study of political language divergence on social media. Machine learning and LLMs are only the researchers' method, and there is no education setting.
Consumer reactions to chatbot communication styles after service failure; not education.
The abstract mixes ChatGPT in academic research with a survey of school students on innovative thinking. It is unclear whether students used AI or learned about it.
